question: The Partition of Bengal in 1905 was carried out by which Viceroy of India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lord Curzon.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Partition of Bengal was conceived and executed by Lord Curzon, Viceroy from 1899 to 1905, and it came into effect on 16 October 1905 (लॉर्ड कर्जन — बंगाल विभाजन के सूत्रधार)

 

• Officially Curzon justified the step on grounds of administrative convenience, because the Bengal Presidency, with Bihar, Odisha and Assam, had become too large to govern.

 

• The real motive was political: to weaken Bengali nationalism, since Bengal was the nerve centre of the national movement, and to divide Hindus from Muslims.

 

• The new province of Eastern Bengal and Assam had a Muslim majority, while the rump Bengal kept a Hindu majority, which sharpened communal feeling.

 

• The decision was announced on 20 July 1905 and drew immediate mass protest, leading directly to the Swadeshi and Boycott movements.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Curzon also carried out the Universities Act (1904), the Indian Official Secrets Act (1904) and created the North-West Frontier Province in 1901.

 

• The partition was annulled in 1911 at the Delhi Durbar by George V on the advice of Viceroy Hardinge.

 

• Congress sessions of 1905 (Banaras) and 1906 (Calcutta) endorsed boycott and Swadeshi in reaction to the partition.

 

• The Muslim League was born in 1906 partly in the atmosphere created by this partition.

 

NOTE

 

• Lord Minto (Option 1): Lord Minto became Viceroy in November 1905, after the partition had already been announced and notified, and is remembered instead for the Indian Councils Act of 1909 granting separate electorates.

 

• Lord Hardinge (Option 2): Lord Hardinge served from 1910 to 1916; far from carrying out the partition, he presided over its annulment in 1911 and over the transfer of the capital to Delhi.

 

• Lord Ripon (Option 4): Lord Ripon governed from 1880 to 1884, a generation earlier, and is known for liberal measures such as the Local Self-Government resolution of 1882 and repeal of the Vernacular Press Act.

question: Dadabhai Naoroji explained the Drain of Wealth theory in which of his works?
option_1: Poverty and Un-British Rule in India
solution_text:
The correct answer is Poverty and Un-British Rule in India.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Dadabhai Naoroji set out his Drain Theory in Poverty and Un-British Rule in India, published in 1901 (पॉवर्टी एंड अन-ब्रिटिश रूल इन इंडिया — नौरोजी का धन निष्कासन सिद्धांत)

 

• He argued that a large portion of India's wealth flowed to Britain without return, through salaries, savings, pensions of British officials, payments to British troops stationed in India, and profits of British companies.

 

• Naoroji called the process an un-British feature of rule, because it contradicted the pledge of fair play that Indians expected from the British.

 

• He was called the Grand Old Man of India and was the first Indian to be elected to the British House of Commons (1892, Finsbury).

 

• The Moderates used the drain argument to build a national consciousness about colonial exploitation.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Naoroji founded the East India Association in London in 1866 and was President of the Congress three times, in 1886, 1893 and 1906.

 

• The Economic History of India by R.C. Dutt (1901-03) is the other classic economic critique of colonial rule.

 

• Naoroji first presented the drain idea in 1867 in a paper titled England's Debt to India.

 

• Other economic nationalists included Justice Ranade, G. Subramania Aiyar and Gopal Krishna Gokhale.

 

NOTE

 

• The Economic History of India (Option 2): The Economic History of India was written by Romesh Chunder Dutt, who documented the decline of Indian industries and the burden of land revenue, not by Naoroji, so it is a different author's work.

 

• India Today (Option 3): India Today was written by the Marxist historian R. Palme Dutt in 1940; it analyses colonialism from a Marxist standpoint and appeared many decades after Naoroji's drain argument.

 

• Unhappy India (Option 4): Unhappy India was written by Lala Lajpat Rai in 1928 as a reply to Katherine Mayo's Mother India; it deals with Indian society and politics rather than the drain of wealth.

question: Dadabhai Naoroji became the first Indian member of which Commission, set up in 1895 to enquire into Indian expenditure?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Welby Commission.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Welby Commission (Royal Commission on Indian Expenditure) was appointed in 1895 under Lord Welby, and Dadabhai Naoroji served on it as an Indian member (वेल्बी आयोग — भारतीय व्यय की जाँच, दादाभाई नौरोजी सदस्य)

 

• Pressure from the Moderates, who had long argued that Indian revenues were being drained to Britain, forced the British Government to set up the enquiry.

 

• Naoroji used the platform to press the Drain Theory, though the Commission's majority report offered little relief on the unfair division of military and home charges.

 

• Gopal Krishna Gokhale and G. Subramania Aiyar also gave evidence before it, which gave the Moderates a visible role in economic criticism of the Raj.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Welby Commission is the standard link between Naoroji and the economic critique of British rule.

 

• The Hunter Commission of 1882 dealt with education, and the Hunter Committee of 1919 enquired into the Punjab disturbances.

 

• The Lee Commission (1924) looked at the Indian civil services, while the Simon Commission (1927) reviewed the working of the 1919 Act and was boycotted for being all-white.

 

NOTE

 

• Hunter Commission (Option 1): The Hunter Commission was the Indian Education Commission of 1882, which stressed primary education and looked at schooling rather than the financial relationship between India and Britain.

 

• Lee Commission (Option 3): The Lee Commission was appointed in 1923 and reported in 1924, dealing with the Indianisation and superior services of the civil administration, a generation after the expenditure enquiry that included Naoroji.

 

• Simon Commission (Option 4): The Simon Commission came in 1927 to review constitutional progress, had no Indian member at all, and was boycotted by Indians; it therefore cannot be the body in which Naoroji sat.

question: Who presided over the 1906 Calcutta Session of the Indian National Congress, where Swaraj was spoken of as the goal for the first time from the Congress platform?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Dadabhai Naoroji.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The 1906 Calcutta Session was presided over by Dadabhai Naoroji, who declared Swaraj (self-government like the United Kingdom or the colonies) to be the aim of the Congress (1906 कलकत्ता अधिवेशन — अध्यक्ष दादाभाई नौरोजी)

 

• Aggressive nationalists, led by Tilak, pressed the aged Moderate to speak of Swaraj, a term that did not form part of the Moderate vocabulary of the time.

 

• The session also adopted resolutions on Boycott, Swadeshi and National Education, which were measures of the Swadeshi agitation against the partition of Bengal.

 

• This was Naoroji's third term as Congress President, after 1886 and 1893, which is a distinction no earlier president had.

 

• The compromise could not hold for long, as the two groups interpreted Swaraj and boycott very differently, which paved the way to the 1907 Surat Split.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Gokhale presided at the Banaras Session of 1905 and criticised Curzon's partition.

 

• Naoroji's three presidencies came in 1886 (Calcutta), 1893 (Lahore) and 1906 (Calcutta).

 

• The resolution on Swaraj was meant to satisfy the Extremists without giving up the constitutional approach of the Moderates.

 

• The next session, at Surat in 1907, was presided over by Rash Behari Ghosh after a bitter dispute over the chair.

 

NOTE

 

• Gopal Krishna Gokhale (Option 1): Gopal Krishna Gokhale was President at Banaras in 1905, a year before; his session condemned the partition and backed Swadeshi in a moderate way but did not carry the Swaraj declaration.

 

• Pherozeshah Mehta (Option 2): Pherozeshah Mehta presided at Calcutta in 1890 and was a key organiser of the Congress in Bombay, but he did not preside in 1906 and in fact opposed the Extremist demands.

 

• Surendranath Banerjee (Option 4): Surendranath Banerjee presided at Pune in 1895 and Ahmedabad in 1902; he led the anti-partition agitation in Bengal but was not the chair at the 1906 session.

question: The Swadeshi Movement was formally launched on 7 August 1905 at a meeting held in
solution_text:
The correct answer is Calcutta Town Hall.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Swadeshi and Boycott movement was formally proclaimed on 7 August 1905 at a mass meeting in the Calcutta Town Hall, where the Boycott resolution was passed (कलकत्ता टाउन हॉल — स्वदेशी आंदोलन की औपचारिक शुरुआत)

 

• The meeting came after the official decision on the partition (20 July 1905) and called for boycott of Manchester cloth and other British goods.

 

• The movement lasted roughly 1905 to 1911, ending with the annulment of the partition, and was both a political and an economic campaign.

 

• Its programme included boycott of government service, courts, schools, colleges and foreign goods, along with the promotion of Swadeshi and national education.

 

• Leaders such as Surendranath Banerjee, Bipin Chandra Pal, Aurobindo and Krishna Kumar Mitra, whose paper Sanjivani spread the message, shaped the agitation.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Partition itself came into force on 16 October 1905, when it was observed as a day of mourning and Rakhi Bandhan was held.

 

• The Swadeshi spirit led to Bengal Chemicals (1901), Tata Steel (1907) and many national schools, including the Bengal National College (1906).

 

• The Indian flag in tricolour and Abanindranath Tagore's painting Bharat Mata date from the Swadeshi age.

 

• Gandhi later called the Swadeshi spirit the soul of Swaraj.

 

NOTE

 

• Dacca Ahsan Manzil (Option 2): Ahsan Manzil in Dacca was the palace of Nawab Salimullah, who supported the partition, so it was not a venue of the boycott proclamation; Dacca was to be capital of Eastern Bengal and Assam.

 

• Benaras Bhelupur (Option 3): Benaras hosted the Congress session of December 1905 under Gokhale, which endorsed the boycott after the formal proclamation had already been made in Calcutta four months earlier.

 

• Pune Shaniwar Wada (Option 4): Shaniwar Wada in Pune is the old Peshwa palace and has no link with the proclamation of Swadeshi, though Tilak did spread the movement in Maharashtra and Pune through Ganapati and Shivaji festivals.

question: The Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company, set up in 1906 to challenge the British shipping monopoly, was founded by
solution_text:
The correct answer is V.O. Chidambaram Pillai.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• V.O. Chidambaram Pillai (V.O.C.) founded the Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company at Tuticorin in 1906 to run ships between Tuticorin and Colombo (वी.ओ. चिदंबरम पिल्लै — स्वदेशी स्टीम नेविगेशन कंपनी)

 

• The venture challenged the British India Steam Navigation Company's monopoly, and was an economic expression of the Swadeshi spirit in the south.

 

• V.O.C. was an Extremist follower of Tilak and led strikes of Tuticorin mill workers, for which he was arrested for sedition in 1908.

 

• He was sentenced to long imprisonment, and his ships were later sold off, but he is remembered in Tamil Nadu as Kappalottiya Tamilan (the Tamil who steered the ship).

 

• The Swadeshi movement therefore spread beyond Bengal, reaching Madras, Maharashtra and Punjab.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Subramania Bharati, the Tamil poet, wrote patriotic songs and was a friend of V.O.C. in the Extremist camp.

 

• Other Swadeshi enterprises included Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works (P.C. Ray, 1901).

 

• The 1908 Tuticorin and Tirunelveli riots followed the arrest of V.O.C. and Subramania Siva.

 

• The Tuticorin millworkers' strike of 1908 was also led by V.O.C. along with Subramania Siva, and both leaders were jailed.

 

NOTE

 

• Subramania Bharati (Option 1): Subramania Bharati was a Tamil poet and journalist whose verses stirred nationalists, but he supported the company morally rather than founding it; he was a friend and associate of the founder.

 

• Lala Lajpat Rai (Option 2): Lala Lajpat Rai was the Punjab leader of the Lal-Bal-Pal trio, associated with the Punjab National Bank (1894) and Arya Samaj institutions rather than any steamship venture in Tuticorin.

 

• Bipin Chandra Pal (Option 4): Bipin Chandra Pal was the Bengal member of the trio and toured south India in 1907 promoting Swaraj, but the shipping company was launched by a local Tamil leader, not by him.

question: The All-India Muslim League was founded in December 1906 at
solution_text:
The correct answer is Dacca.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The All-India Muslim League was set up on 30 December 1906 at Dacca, during the sitting of the All India Muhammadan Educational Conference (ढाका — मुस्लिम लीग की स्थापना, 1906)

 

• Nawab Salimullah of Dacca proposed the formation of a political body to protect Muslim interests, and the proposal was accepted by delegates from all over India.

 

• Other leaders at the founding included Aga Khan, Nawab Mohsin-ul-Mulk and Waqar-ul-Mulk; Aga Khan became the first (honorary) President.

 

• The League enjoyed British encouragement and supported the Partition of Bengal while opposing the Swadeshi movement.

 

• Its first major political gain was separate electorates for Muslims under the Minto-Morley Reforms of 1909.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• A Muslim deputation led by the Aga Khan had met Viceroy Minto at Simla in October 1906 and demanded separate representation.

 

• Jinnah joined the League only in 1913, and the 1916 Lucknow Pact was its first joint understanding with the Congress.

 

• The League's later headquarters shifted to Lucknow, which hosted the 1916 session where the pact was signed.

 

• The Lahore Session of 1940 passed the Pakistan Resolution.

 

NOTE

 

• Lucknow (Option 2): Lucknow hosted the League's session in 1916, when the Pact with Congress was concluded, but the organisation had already existed for ten years by then and was formed elsewhere.

 

• Lahore (Option 3): Lahore is associated with the 1940 Resolution demanding Pakistan and with the Congress Purna Swaraj session of 1929, not with the founding of the League in the first decade of the century.

 

• Aligarh (Option 4): Aligarh was the home of the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College founded by Syed Ahmad Khan, and the League's leaders came from there, but the actual founding took place at the Dacca conference.

question: Who was the first (honorary) President of the All-India Muslim League?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Aga Khan III.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sir Sultan Muhammad Shah, Aga Khan III, was the first (honorary) President of the All-India Muslim League formed in 1906 (आगा खां तृतीय — मुस्लिम लीग के प्रथम अध्यक्ष)

 

• He led the Simla Deputation to Viceroy Minto in October 1906, asking for separate electorates and weightage for Muslims in the councils.

 

• Nawab Salimullah of Dacca only proposed the idea of the organisation; he was a prominent founder-member but not its first President.

 

• Waqar-ul-Mulk and Mohsin-ul-Mulk helped to organise the League, and Waqar-ul-Mulk later led it as Secretary in the early years.

 

• Jinnah, who joined in 1913, took over the League only later, and the great Lucknow Pact of 1916 brought him to prominence.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The League's initial programme was loyalty to the British Government, protection of Muslim interests and avoiding hostility to other communities.

 

• The Aga Khan was later India's representative at the League of Nations and the Round Table Conferences.

 

• The 1909 Morley-Minto Reforms recognised separate electorates, which was the first concrete success of the League.

 

• Syed Ahmad Khan (1817-1898) had earlier urged Muslims to stay aloof from the Congress.

 

NOTE

 

• Muhammad Ali Jinnah (Option 1): Muhammad Ali Jinnah entered the League in 1913 and was President in 1916 and again from 1934 onwards, so he could not have been the head at its inception in 1906 when he was still in the Congress.

 

• Nawab Salimullah (Option 2): Nawab Salimullah of Dacca proposed the League at the Educational Conference and strongly supported the partition, yet the honorary presidency at the start went to a different leader, the Aga Khan.

 

• Syed Ahmad Khan (Option 4): Syed Ahmad Khan died in 1898, eight years before the League was formed, so he cannot have headed it; he is known for founding the Aligarh movement and opposing the Congress.

question: The 1907 session of the Indian National Congress, at which the party split into the Moderates and Extremists, was held at
solution_text:
The correct answer is Surat.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Surat Session of December 1907 ended in the Surat Split, with the Extremists led by Tilak, Lajpat Rai and Bipin Chandra Pal leaving the Congress (सूरत अधिवेशन 1907 — कांग्रेस में विभाजन)

 

• The Moderates wanted Rash Behari Ghosh as President, while the Extremists backed Lala Lajpat Rai; the venue itself had first been planned at Nagpur and then shifted to Surat.

 

• The dispute was over Boycott, Swadeshi, national education and Swaraj, which the Moderates treated as unconstitutional extremes.

 

• After the split, the Moderates held a separate meeting and reaffirmed the objective of self-government within the British Empire by constitutional methods only.

 

• The Government encouraged the divide and soon cracked down on the Extremists, with Tilak imprisoned in 1908.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Congress remained under Moderate control until the reunion at the Lucknow Session of 1916.

 

• Rash Behari Ghosh presided at Surat in 1907 and again at Madras in 1908.

 

• Surat is also the place of the Treaty of Surat (1775) and a trading factory of the English East India Company (1608).

 

• Tilak was tried for sedition in 1908 and sent to Mandalay jail for six years.

 

NOTE

 

• Nagpur (Option 1): Nagpur was the first intended venue for the 1907 session, but it was shifted for the dispute over the presidency; the Nagpur Congress of 1920 later approved Non-Cooperation under Gandhi.

 

• Madras (Option 3): Madras hosted the 1908 session, held after the split, where only the Moderates attended and they adopted a new constitution; it did not witness the confrontation itself.

 

• Lahore (Option 4): Lahore saw the 1929 Purna Swaraj resolution under Nehru, more than two decades later; the Lahore Congress of 1893 under Naoroji had no connection with the 1907 break.

question: The Delhi Durbar of 1911 was held to mark the coronation of which British monarch?
solution_text:
The correct answer is George V.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Delhi Durbar of 1911 was organised to celebrate the succession of King George V as Emperor of India, and it was held when Lord Hardinge was Viceroy (जॉर्ज पंचम — 1911 का दिल्ली दरबार)

 

• At the Durbar the King announced the annulment of the Partition of Bengal and the transfer of the imperial capital from Calcutta to Delhi.

 

• The annulment satisfied Bengali agitators, but the creation of a Muslim-majority province was cancelled, which disappointed Muslims who had favoured the partition.

 

• Three Durbars were held in total, in 1877 (Lytton, Queen Victoria as Empress), 1903 (Curzon, Edward VII) and 1911 (Hardinge, George V).

 

• Bihar and Orissa were also carved out of Bengal as a separate province, and the Durbar thus reshaped the political map of eastern India.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• George V and Queen Mary visited India in person for the 1911 Durbar, the only reigning monarch to attend a Durbar in India.

 

• The foundation stone of New Delhi was laid in 1911, and the city was inaugurated in 1931 with Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker as architects.

 

• The Coronation Park in Delhi marks the Durbar site.

 

• Calcutta had been the capital since 1772 under Warren Hastings and then the capital of British India from 1858.

 

NOTE

 

• Edward VII (Option 1): Edward VII was crowned in 1902 and was proclaimed Emperor at the 1903 Durbar, held by Curzon; he had died in 1910, before the 1911 gathering that announced the partition's annulment.

 

• George VI (Option 2): George VI came to the throne only in 1936, after the abdication of his brother, and the Durbar tradition had ended by then, so he cannot be associated with the 1911 ceremony.

 

• Edward VIII (Option 4): Edward VIII reigned for less than a year in 1936 and was never crowned; he belongs to a later period than the Delhi Durbar of 1911, which honoured his father.

question: The Gadar Party, formed in 1913 in America, was founded by
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lala Hardayal.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Gadar Party (Hindustan Association of the Pacific Coast) was founded in 1913 at San Francisco by Lala Hardayal with its headquarters in the Yugantar Ashram (लाला हरदयाल — गदर पार्टी के संस्थापक, 1913)

 

• Sohan Singh Bhakna became the first President of the party, while Hardayal was its general secretary and chief ideologue.

 

• The party published a newspaper, Gadar, in Urdu, Punjabi and other languages, and the name recalled the revolt of 1857.

 

• Its members were mostly Punjabi Sikh immigrants in the USA and Canada, and they planned an armed revolt in India during the First World War.

 

• The Komagata Maru incident of 1914 and the Ghadar conspiracy of 1915 mark the highpoint of the movement.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Ghadar plot of February 1915 was betrayed by an informer, leading to the Lahore Conspiracy Case and executions, including Kartar Singh Sarabha.

 

• Lala Hardayal later left the party and wrote Forty-Four Months in Germany and Turkey.

 

• Rash Behari Bose tried to organise the 1915 revolt in India and later founded the Indian Independence League in Japan.

 

• The Gadar movement is the best-known overseas revolutionary organisation before 1920.

 

NOTE

 

• Ras Behari Bose (Option 1): Rash Behari Bose was a Bengal revolutionary who threw the bomb at Viceroy Hardinge in Delhi in 1912 and later fled to Japan, but he did not set up the Gadar Party in the United States.

 

• Sohan Singh Bhakna (Option 3): Sohan Singh Bhakna was the first President of the party and a leader of Punjabi immigrants; he was its head rather than the founder who conceived and launched the association with Hardayal.

 

• Bhagwan Singh Gyanee (Option 4): Bhagwan Singh Gyanee was a Sikh preacher and associate in the Gadar movement in the Pacific coast and Hong Kong, but the credit for founding the party is given to Hardayal.

question: Which Muslim leader proposed the formation of an all-India organisation to look after Muslim interests at the Dacca meeting of December 1906?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Nawab Salimullah.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Nawab Salimullah of Dacca put forward the proposal for a political organisation of Muslims at the Muhammadan Educational Conference in 1906, which led to the formation of the Muslim League (नवाब सलीमुल्ला — ढाका के नवाब, मुस्लिम लीग के प्रस्तावक)

 

• He was an influential landlord who strongly supported the Partition of Bengal, since it created a Muslim-majority province with Dacca as capital.

 

• The British Government is said to have given him a large loan to encourage his political activity against the Swadeshi agitation.

 

• The proposal was accepted, and the All-India Muslim League was formally set up on 30 December 1906 with Aga Khan as the honorary President.

 

• The creation of a separate Muslim political body reflected a growing communal turn in politics, helped by official policy.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Salimullah's family palace, Ahsan Manzil, is now a museum in Dhaka.

 

• The Muslim League chose to oppose Swadeshi and boycott and to stay loyal to the British Government at the beginning.

 

• Waqar-ul-Mulk was another founder and later became Secretary of the League.

 

• The first achievement of the League was the grant of separate electorates in 1909.

 

NOTE

 

• Hakim Ajmal Khan (Option 2): Hakim Ajmal Khan was a physician and nationalist who later headed the Congress session of 1921 and was a leader of the Khilafat movement; he took no part in proposing the League at Dacca.

 

• Muhammad Iqbal (Option 3): Muhammad Iqbal, the poet, was in Europe in 1905-08 and was not linked with the founding; he is known for his 1930 Allahabad address that envisaged a Muslim state in north-western India.

 

• Maulana Shaukat Ali (Option 4): Maulana Shaukat Ali, with his brother Muhammad Ali, became prominent in the Khilafat movement after 1919, long after the League's formation, and was not the proposer at Dacca.

question: The Lucknow Pact of 1916 was an agreement between the
option_3: Congress and the Home Rule League
option_4: Muslim League and the Hindu Mahasabha
solution_text:
The correct answer is Congress and the Muslim League.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Lucknow Pact (December 1916) was a joint understanding between the Indian National Congress and the All-India Muslim League, concluded at the sessions held at Lucknow (लखनऊ समझौता 1916 — कांग्रेस और मुस्लिम लीग)

 

• Under the pact the Congress accepted separate electorates for Muslims, a concession the League had won in 1909, and agreed to a formula for Muslim representation in the provincial councils.

 

• Both parties placed joint demands before the Government: a larger elected majority in the councils and more self-government for India.

 

• The Congress session was presided over by Ambika Charan Majumdar, while Jinnah and Tilak were architects of the settlement.

 

• The pact marked the high point of Hindu-Muslim unity in the period, but it formally accepted communal politics.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Congress had been reunited in 1916 after the Moderate and Extremist wings came together at the same session.

 

• The Lucknow session held in 1916 also saw the League's meeting under Jinnah as President.

 

• The Government of India Act 1919 incorporated the pact's basic idea of separate Muslim electorates in the provinces.

 

• A few leaders, including Madan Mohan Malaviya, doubted the wisdom of the arrangement.

 

NOTE

 

• Moderates and the British Government (Option 1): The Moderates and the British Government did not sign any such pact; the Moderates were a faction within the Congress, and the Government's own response to Indian demands came later in the August Declaration of 1917.

 

• Congress and the Home Rule League (Option 3): The Home Rule Leagues were propaganda bodies led by Tilak and Annie Besant that worked alongside the Congress; they were not a party to the agreement, which was signed by the two major parties.

 

• Muslim League and the Hindu Mahasabha (Option 4): The Hindu Mahasabha was founded in 1915 but took no part in the 1916 settlement, and the pact is remembered as Congress-League cooperation rather than any arrangement involving the Mahasabha.

question: Who was the first President of Tilak's Indian Home Rule League, established in April 1916?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Joseph Baptista.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Joseph Baptista was the first President of the Indian Home Rule League founded by Tilak in April 1916 at Belgaum (जोसेफ बैप्टिस्टा — तिलक की होमरूल लीग के प्रथम अध्यक्ष)

 

• Tilak's League worked in Maharashtra (excluding Bombay city), Karnataka, the Central Provinces and Berar, with its headquarters at Poona.

 

• Tilak's newspapers Kesari (Marathi) and Mahratta (English) carried the propaganda for Home Rule.

 

• It was the rival of Annie Besant's separate league, which started in September 1916 with Adyar, Madras, as its base and covered the rest of India.

 

• Tilak had returned from Mandalay jail in 1914, and his slogan that Swaraj is a birthright found a new audience through the League.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• N.C. Kelkar was Tilak's close associate and secretary of the Poona league.

 

• George Arundale was Besant's organising secretary, and B.P. Wadia and C.P. Ramaswami Aiyar also helped her League.

 

• The Government banned Home Rule meetings in some areas and interned Besant in June 1917.

 

• In the August Declaration of 1917, Montagu said that responsible government was the goal of British policy.

 

NOTE

 

• N.C. Kelkar (Option 1): N.C. Kelkar was a journalist and Tilak's lieutenant who edited Kesari after him, but the presidency of the League went to Baptista rather than to Kelkar.

 

• G.S. Khaparde (Option 2): G.S. Khaparde was an Extremist from Amravati and Tilak's associate in the Central Provinces, but he is not named as the first head of the Poona-based League.

 

• Annie Besant (Option 4): Annie Besant led a different Home Rule League of her own, started in September 1916; she was not the President of Tilak's League, which was kept distinct from her organisation.

question: Which pair of weeklies was used by Annie Besant to propagate the Home Rule cause?
option_4: <style> @font-face { font-family: 'Patrika'; src: url('https://static-appxdb-v2.akamai.net.in/fonts/Patrika.ttf') format('truetype');} </style>Amrita Bazar Patrika and Hindu
solution_text:
The correct answer is Commonweal and New India.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Annie Besant used the weekly Commonweal and the daily New India (which she took over in 1914) to spread her Home Rule message (कॉमनवील और न्यू इंडिया — एनी बेसेंट के समाचार पत्र)

 

• Her Home Rule League was started in September 1916 at Madras (Adyar) and covered the whole of India except the areas of Tilak's league.

 

• She was an Irish theosophist who had come to India in 1893 and drew inspiration from the Irish Home Rule movement.

 

• Her organisation spread to Madras, Uttar Pradesh, Bengal and Gujarat through a network of branches.

 

• The Government's repression of her, including internment in June 1917, produced a wave of sympathy and widened the movement.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Besant was elected Congress President in 1917 at Calcutta, the first woman to hold the post.

 

• Aim of the League was Home Rule, that is, Dominion status within the British Empire.

 

• Tilak's league ran Kesari and Mahratta, whereas Besant's league was served by Commonweal and New India.

 

• The Home Rule movement contributed to the Montagu Declaration of 1917.

 

NOTE

 

• Kesari and Mahratta (Option 2): Kesari and Mahratta belonged to Bal Gangadhar Tilak and were published from Poona; they served the Home Rule League of Tilak, not that of Annie Besant, which worked with a different publication set.

 

• Bande Mataram and Yugantar (Option 3): Bande Mataram and Yugantar were Bengal-based nationalist papers linked with Aurobindo and the revolutionary group, and they belonged to the Swadeshi era a decade earlier rather than to the Home Rule campaign.

 

• Amrita Bazar Patrika and Hindu (Option 4): Amrita Bazar Patrika and The Hindu were established nationalist dailies from Calcutta and Madras, representing moderate opinion more than the Home Rule agitation that Besant led through her own weeklies.

question: Who edited the English newspaper Bande Mataram, which helped to mobilise public opinion during the Swadeshi movement?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Aurobindo Ghosh.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Aurobindo Ghosh edited the English daily Bande Mataram, started in 1906 by Bipin Chandra Pal, and used it to preach passive resistance and Swaraj (अरविंद घोष — बंदे मातरम के संपादक)

 

• Aurobindo wrote that the aim was complete autonomy free from British control, and he stood for boycott, national education and passive resistance.

 

• He was arrested in the Alipore Bomb Case of 1908 (the attempt on Kingsford, a Magistrate, by Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki) but was acquitted after defence by C.R. Das.

 

• He afterwards retired to Pondicherry and turned to spiritual life, founding the Aurobindo Ashram.

 

• He belonged to the Extremist camp together with Lal-Bal-Pal and criticised the Moderates for their politics of prayer.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The song Vande Mataram comes from Bankim Chandra Chatterjee's novel Anandamath (1882) and was sung at the 1896 Congress session by Tagore.

 

• Aurobindo's journal Karmayogin and his Bengali weekly Dharma were also Swadeshi-era publications.

 

• The Yugantar and Sandhya were other nationalist papers of Bengal.

 

• The English version of Bande Mataram became the first major English-language voice of the Extremists in Bengal.

 

NOTE

 

• Surendranath Banerjee (Option 1): Surendranath Banerjee edited The Bengalee, a leading Moderate paper, and he led the anti-partition agitation, but Bande Mataram was run by the Extremist group around Aurobindo.

 

• Gopal Krishna Gokhale (Option 2): Gopal Krishna Gokhale was a Moderate who founded the Servants of India Society in 1905 and edited the weekly Sudharak; he did not work as the editor of Bande Mataram.

 

• Madan Mohan Malaviya (Option 3): Madan Mohan Malaviya edited the Hindustan and Abhyudaya and founded Banaras Hindu University; his journalism belonged to the United Provinces and Moderate-leaning politics, not the Bengal Extremist paper.

question: Bihar Day is celebrated on 22 March to mark the creation of Bihar as a separate province from the Bengal Presidency in the year
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1912.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Bihar was separated from the Bengal Presidency and constituted as a new province, Bihar and Orissa, on 22 March 1912, which is celebrated every year as Bihar Day (बिहार दिवस — 22 मार्च 1912)

 

• The change followed the Delhi Durbar of December 1911, where George V announced the annulment of the Partition of Bengal and the reorganisation of the eastern provinces.

 

• A Bengali-speaking Bengal Presidency was re-united while Bihar and Orissa were given a Lieutenant Governor's province with its capital at Patna.

 

• The demand for a separate Bihar had been raised for many years by educated Biharis, notably Sachchidananda Sinha.

 

• The final separation of Orissa from Bihar took place on 1 April 1936.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Assam was made a Chief Commissioner's province again in 1912.

 

• The 1911 Durbar announcements were implemented by Lord Hardinge's government in 1912.

 

• Sachchidananda Sinha later became the temporary chairman of the Constituent Assembly in 1946.

 

• Jharkhand was carved out of Bihar only in 2000.

 

• Orissa, which had been joined to Bihar in 1912, became a separate province on 1 April 1936 under the Government of India Act 1935.

 

NOTE

 

• 1905 (Option 1): The year 1905 is when Bengal was partitioned, not when Bihar attained provincial status; in 1905 Bihar remained under Bengal's authority and became part of the unwieldy Presidency discussion.

 

• 1911 (Option 2): In 1911 the annulment of the partition was announced at the Delhi Durbar, but the actual constitution of the new province of Bihar and Orissa followed in the spring of the next year.

 

• 1916 (Option 4): In 1916 the Patna High Court was established and the Lucknow Pact was signed; Bihar had already become a separate province four years earlier, so this year is not correct.

question: The Lucknow Session of the Indian National Congress in 1916 was presided over by
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ambika Charan Majumdar.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The 1916 Lucknow Session was presided over by Ambika Charan Majumdar, a Moderate from Bengal (अंबिका चरण मजूमदार — कांग्रेस का लखनऊ अधिवेशन, 1916)

 

• At this session the Congress was re-united, as the Extremists led by Tilak returned after nine years of separation since the Surat Split.

 

• Under Majumdar's chair the Congress concluded the Lucknow Pact with the Muslim League, accepting separate electorates.

 

• The session also demanded that the Government announce its intention of granting self-government to India after the war.

 

• Tilak's return and the pact together gave Indian politics a new unity going into the Home Rule Movement.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Home Rule Movement of Tilak and Besant ran parallel to this session, in 1916.

 

• Annie Besant was the Congress President at the Calcutta session of 1917.

 

• Rash Behari Ghosh presided at the Congress sessions of 1907 (Surat) and 1908 (Madras).

 

• Gandhi attended the Lucknow session and met Rajkumar Shukla, who pressed him to visit Champaran.

 

NOTE

 

• Annie Besant (Option 1): Annie Besant became President of the Congress in 1917 at Calcutta, the year following; as the first woman president she was elected after the Home Rule agitation had grown.

 

• Rash Behari Ghosh (Option 3): Rash Behari Ghosh was President at the Surat Session of 1907 and the Madras Session of 1908, not at Lucknow; he belonged to the Moderate group that dominated those years.

 

• Bishan Narayan Dar (Option 4): Bishan Narayan Dar presided over the Calcutta session of 1911 and was a Moderate lawyer from Lucknow; though a native of the city, he did not chair the 1916 gathering.

question: Which song, composed by Rabindranath Tagore at the time of the 1905 partition agitation, later became the national anthem of Bangladesh?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Amar Sonar Bangla.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Amar Sonar Bangla was composed by Rabindranath Tagore in 1905 during the anti-partition agitation, and it later became the national anthem of Bangladesh (आमार सोनार बांग्ला — बांग्लादेश का राष्ट्रगान)

 

• Tagore also observed 16 October 1905, the day the partition took effect, as Rakhi Bandhan Day, when Hindus and Muslims tied rakhis on one another's wrists as a symbol of unity.

 

• On that day, people fasted, walked barefoot to bathe in the Ganga and sang Bande Mataram in processions in Calcutta.

 

• Tagore's creative contribution to the Swadeshi age also includes the songs Banglar Mati Banglar Jal and the essay Swadeshi Samaj.

 

• He gave up the Knighthood in 1919 in protest against the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Jana Gana Mana was written by Tagore in 1911 and first sung at the Calcutta Congress session of December 1911; it was adopted as India's national anthem in 1950.

 

• Vande Mataram is a poem by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee, published in the novel Anandamath.

 

• Tagore's Gitanjali won him the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913.

 

• The Swadeshi age also saw the foundation of Bengal National College, with Aurobindo as the first principal.

 

NOTE

 

• Jana Gana Mana (Option 2): Jana Gana Mana is a different composition by Tagore, first performed in 1911, and is India's national anthem; it is not the song for the partition protest that became Bangladesh's anthem.

 

• Vande Mataram (Option 3): Vande Mataram was written by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee in the 1870s and became the rallying cry of the movement, but its author is Bankim and it is a national song of India.

 

• Ekla Chalo Re (Option 4): Ekla Chalo Re is another of Tagore's patriotic songs, urging a lone traveller to go on despite no company; it is celebrated, but it is not the national anthem of Bangladesh.

question: The August Declaration of 1917 in the British Parliament was made by
solution_text:
The correct answer is Edwin Montagu.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The August Declaration of 20 August 1917 was made in the House of Commons by Edwin Montagu, the Secretary of State for India (एडविन मॉन्टेग्यू — अगस्त घोषणा 1917)

 

• It stated that British policy was the gradual development of self-governing institutions and the progressive realisation of responsible government in India as an integral part of the Empire.

 

• The Home Rule Movement is credited with pushing the Government to this statement, which implied that the demand for Home Rule was no longer to be considered seditious.

 

• Montagu then visited India and, with Viceroy Chelmsford, prepared the Montagu-Chelmsford Report (1918) leading to the Government of India Act 1919.

 

• Besant, interned in June 1917, was released after the declaration and was elected Congress President.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The declaration is also called the Montagu Declaration.

 

• The Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms introduced dyarchy in the provinces.

 

• Chelmsford was the Viceroy from 1916 to 1921.

 

• The Government of India Act 1919 provided for a bicameral central legislature.

 

• The declaration was a response to wartime pressure, since India had supplied soldiers and resources to Britain during the First World War.

 

NOTE

 

• Lord Chelmsford (Option 1): Lord Chelmsford was the Viceroy from 1916 to 1921 and co-authored the report on reforms, but the announcement in Parliament was made by the Secretary of State, not the Viceroy.

 

• Lord Hardinge (Option 2): Lord Hardinge had completed his term as Viceroy in 1916; his major acts, the annulment of the partition and transfer of the capital, belong to 1911 and not the declaration of 1917.

 

• Lord Minto (Option 3): Lord Minto was Viceroy from 1905 to 1910 and associated with the Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909; he held no office in 1917 and had no hand in this announcement.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Moderate phase (1885-1905) of the Congress.

1. The Moderates had faith in British justice and fair play.

2. They aimed to attain self-government by stages through constitutional agitation.

3. They advocated boycott of government schools and courts.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: the Moderates trusted the British sense of justice and fair play and looked to England for inspiration and guidance (नरमपंथी — ब्रिटिश न्याय में विश्वास, संवैधानिक तरीके)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: their aim was to win political rights and self-government stage by stage, through petitions, prayers and protests within the law.

 

• Statement 3 is incorrect: boycott of courts, schools and colleges, along with passive resistance, was a technique of the Extremists during the Swadeshi movement after 1905.

 

• The Moderates also confined political activity to the educated middle class and tried to build national unity transcending caste, religion and province.

 

• Their economic critique, notably Naoroji's Drain Theory, exposed the exploitative nature of colonial rule.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Moderate leaders included W.C. Bonnerjee, Surendranath Banerjee, Dadabhai Naoroji, Pherozeshah Mehta, Gokhale, Malaviya, Badruddin Tyabji, Justice Ranade and G. Subramania Aiyar.

 

• Their methods are commonly summed up as the 'politics of petitions and prayers'.

 

• The Moderate period is placed from 1885 to 1905, followed by the Extremist phase from 1905 to 1916-17.

 

• In its early years the British welcomed the Congress, and Dufferin hosted a garden party for its delegates in 1886.

 

NOTE

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 1): The combination of statements 2 and 3 is wrong, because statement 3 attributes boycott of courts and schools to the Moderates, who actually disapproved of such confrontational methods and relied on constitutional appeals.

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 3): Pairing statements 1 and 3 fails for the same reason, since it leaves out the correct statement 2 and keeps the incorrect one about boycott of institutions, which was the Extremist line.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Accepting all three statements cannot be right, as statement 3 contradicts the cautious and loyal approach of the Moderate leadership; boycott became a Congress slogan only after the partition of Bengal.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Extremists in the Indian National Congress.

1. Their objective was Swaraj rather than mere self-government.

2. They supported non-cooperation through boycott of schools and courts.

3. They believed that the British could be trusted to grant reforms voluntarily.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: the Extremists made Swaraj, or independence, their main goal, rather than the self-government stage by stage sought by the Moderates (उग्रवादी — स्वराज का लक्ष्य)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: they used non-cooperation with the Government, boycott of courts, schools and colleges and foreign goods, and promoted Swadeshi and national education.

 

• Statement 3 is incorrect: the Extremists distrusted British intentions and rejected the 'politics of prayer', insisting that freedom had to be won through self-reliance and sacrifice.

 

• Their well-known leaders were the Lal-Bal-Pal trio, Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal, together with Aurobindo Ghosh.

 

• Tilak's cry that Swaraj is his birthright and he shall have it was a rallying call of this phase.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The immediate cause for the rise of Extremism was Curzon's reactionary rule and the partition of Bengal.

 

• Other causes include dissatisfaction with Moderate achievements and the ill-treatment of Indians in South Africa.

 

• The Extremist phase is dated 1905-1916 in the notes of this chapter.

 

• Tilak was jailed for six years in 1908 after writing in Kesari in support of the Muzaffarpur bomb throwers.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 only (Option 1): Choosing statement 1 alone would leave out the boycott and non-cooperation approach, which is also a genuine characteristic of the Extremists as seen during the Swadeshi movement.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 2): The combination of statements 2 and 3 wrongly credits the Extremists with trust in the British; reliance on British goodwill was the Moderate stance that they had criticised.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Taking all three as correct fails because of statement 3, since the Extremists openly denounced faith in the sense of British justice as a futile 'mendicancy' that had yielded little.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Partition of Bengal (1905).

1. It was carried out under Viceroy Lord Curzon.

2. It created a province of Eastern Bengal and Assam with a Muslim majority.

3. It was cancelled at the Delhi Durbar of 1911.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1, 2 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: Lord Curzon conceived and enforced the partition, which took effect on 16 October 1905 after the announcement on 20 July (कर्जन — बंगाल विभाजन 1905)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: Bengal was divided so that East Bengal and Assam became Muslim-majority while the west retained a Hindu majority, which was meant to divide the two communities.

 

• Statement 3 is correct: following widespread protest, the partition was annulled in 1911 and announced by King George V at the Delhi Durbar under Viceroy Hardinge.

 

• The annulment came together with the shift of the capital from Calcutta to Delhi and the carving out of Bihar and Orissa the following year.

 

• Despite this, the episode left a lasting communal impact.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The partition provoked the Swadeshi movement, the boycott of foreign goods and the first big mass mobilisation of the freedom struggle.

 

• Tagore's Rakhi Bandhan on the day it came into force was meant to show Hindu-Muslim brotherhood.

 

• Muslim League formation in 1906 is linked partly with it.

 

• The area covered by old Bengal included present West Bengal, Bihar, Odisha, Bangladesh and Assam.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 and 2 only (Option 1): Statements 1 and 2 are both right, but the combination ignores statement 3, which is also true: the partition did not last, and the Delhi Durbar of 1911 cancelled it.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 2): The pair of the Muslim-majority province and the 1911 cancellation is right but leave out statement 1; Curzon was undoubtedly the Viceroy who carried out the partition, so excluding it makes the combination incomplete.

 

• 3 only (Option 3): Statement 3 on its own is true but incomplete, since the first two statements about Curzon and the Muslim-majority province of Eastern Bengal and Assam are equally accurate.

question:
Consider the following statements regarding the Swadeshi Movement.

1. It was formally launched on 7 August 1905 in the Calcutta Town Hall.

2. Krishna Kumar Mitra's journal Sanjivani popularised the idea of boycott.

3. It had widespread participation from the peasantry.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: the Boycott resolution of 7 August 1905 at the Calcutta Town Hall formally began the Swadeshi movement (स्वदेशी आंदोलन — 7 अगस्त 1905)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: Krishna Kumar Mitra, through his paper Sanjivani, stressed national education, boycott and economic self-sufficiency.

 

• Statement 3 is incorrect: the movement is known for its limited peasant participation, because it did not address specific peasant grievances and remained largely urban and middle-class.

 

• Other weaknesses were lack of organisation and the failure to carry Muslims, made worse by the Muslim League's opposition.

 

• Its achievements were national schools and colleges, Swadeshi enterprises and a lasting culture of boycott.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Swadeshi programmes included boycott of government service, courts, schools, colleges and foreign goods.

 

• Abanindranath Tagore's Bharat Mata painting dates from 1905.

 

• The movement ran roughly from 1905 to 1911.

 

• Bipin Chandra Pal and Aurobindo were prominent advocates, and the Samiti groups of Bengal such as Swadesh Bandhab Samiti of Ashwini Kumar Dutta in Barisal were active.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 2): The combination of statements 1 and 3 is wrong because statement 3 misses the main weakness of the movement, which could not draw in the peasants whose specific problems it never took up.

 

• 2 only (Option 3): Statement 2 alone is true but incomplete, since the launch on 7 August 1905 at the Town Hall in Calcutta is equally correct and widely stated as the formal start of the campaign.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): All three cannot be right, as the movement is remembered for failing to involve the peasantry in large numbers; this is listed among its challenges, along with lack of organisation.

question:
With reference to the Muslim League, consider the following statements.

1. It supported the Partition of Bengal and opposed the Swadeshi movement.

2. Its first success was the grant of separate electorates in the Minto-Morley Reforms.

3. Muhammad Ali Jinnah was among its founders in 1906.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: the League backed the Partition of Bengal, which gave Muslims a majority province, and it actively opposed the Swadeshi movement (मुस्लिम लीग — बंग-भंग का समर्थन)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: the Indian Councils Act 1909 (Minto-Morley Reforms) conceded separate electorates for Muslims, the League's first achievement.

 

• Statement 3 is incorrect: Jinnah joined the League only in 1913; at its founding he was still a Congress member, and the founders were Aga Khan, Nawab Salimullah and Waqar-ul-Mulk.

 

• The League was founded on 30 December 1906 at Dacca, with Aga Khan as its first honorary President.

 

• It enjoyed British patronage in the early years, but it moved closer to the Congress in 1916.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Jinnah served as the Congress and League member, earning the title 'Ambassador of Hindu-Muslim Unity' for the 1916 pact.

 

• Like the Congress, the League held annual sessions and placed demands before the British.

 

• The Minto-Morley Reforms are named for Viceroy Minto and Secretary of State Morley.

 

• Separate electorates were extended to Sikhs, Indian Christians and others by the 1919 and 1935 Acts.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 only (Option 1): Statement 1 alone ignores the League's success in getting separate electorates, which is a documented outcome of the 1909 reforms and the first political gain it secured.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 2): Joining the separate-electorate point with Jinnah's role goes wrong, because Jinnah was not a founder in 1906; he joined the League in 1913, a full seven years later, after leaving his earlier loyalty to the Congress.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): Taking all three statements is not possible, since Jinnah's association began only in 1913; he is not counted among those who established the body at Dacca.
